The user now wants multiplayer support with a lobby and also wants performance optimizations because the game runs slowly. I've already set up a basic WebSocket server (server.js) and added a client networking module (net.js). The next logical piece is to share the soldier model code between the host, bots, and remote players, so that both AI and networked players use the same low‑poly geometry and materials. This will also let me later replace the existing per‑enemy model creation with calls to a common builder, reducing duplicated code and potentially improving memory usage.

First, I need to create a new module in the src folder that can be imported wherever a soldier (player or bot) is needed. It should expose two functions:

1. `buildSoldier(group, kind)` – builds the meshes, sets up hitboxes, and returns references (head, muzzle, legs) needed for hit detection and shooting. It should accept a `kind` parameter to allow different color palettes (hostile, blue, red) for team differentiation. I’ll define a palette object with appropriate hex colors, then cache the generated materials per kind to avoid creating new material instances each time a soldier is built. This caching is important for performance because material creation is expensive and we may have many soldiers.

2. `makeNameTag(text, color)` – creates a canvas‑based sprite to display player names above heads. This will be useful for multiplayer to identify each remote player.

I’ll implement the material cache (`matCache`) and a helper `mats(kind)` that lazily creates the four materials (cloth, vest, skin, gun) using `THREE.MeshStandardMaterial` with suitable roughness and metalness values. The colors come from the palette; if an unknown kind is passed, fallback to the hostile palette.

Inside `buildSoldier`, I’ll define an `add` helper that creates a mesh from a geometry and material, positions it, enables casting shadows, optionally tags it as a hitbox part, and adds it to the provided `group`. I’ll also collect hitbox meshes in an array for later collision checks.

Then I’ll construct the body parts using simple box geometries, matching the dimensions used elsewhere in the project. I’ll add legs, torso, vest, arms, head, helmet, and a gun mesh. For the gun I won’t add it to hitboxes (null part). I’ll also create a separate `Object3D` for the muzzle location, positioned at the end of the rifle, and add it to the group.

Finally, I’ll return an object containing the hitboxes array and references to key parts (head, muzzle, legL, legR) that the rest of the code will need for aiming and hit detection.

For the name tag, I’ll create a canvas, draw stroked and filled text with the provided color, turn it into a `THREE.CanvasTexture`, set its color space, and create a sprite with a `SpriteMaterial`. I’ll scale and position the sprite above the soldier’s head and set a high render order so it appears on top.

All of this belongs in a new file `src/soldier.js`. I’ll write the full content as a string to the `Write` tool, targeting that path. This addition completes the shared soldier builder needed for both bots and networked players, and the material caching will help with the performance concerns the user raised.
